q1.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE economic motive for European imperialism in the period c. 1750 to c. 1900.
parts.b: Explain ONE way in which Social Darwinist ideas were used to justify imperialism, using the historian's interpretation in the passage.
parts.c: Explain ONE way in which colonized peoples challenged imperialist ideology in the period c. 1750 to c. 1900.

sample_answers.a: Industrial economies needed secure supplies of raw materials such as cotton, rubber, and minerals, and sought captive markets for manufactured goods; colonies promised both, along with profitable investment opportunities for surplus capital.
sample_answers.b: According to the passage, imperialists borrowed Darwin's language of natural selection to claim that European dominance proved European superiority, turning military and technological advantage into a supposed law of nature that made empire seem inevitable and right.
sample_answers.c: Colonized intellectuals and leaders exposed the gap between imperialist claims of civilization and the violence of conquest — for example, Indian nationalists argued that British rule impoverished India rather than uplifting it, directly contradicting the 'civilizing mission.'

q1.stimulus:
Historians emphasize that European imperialism in the late nineteenth century was justified by a powerful set of ideas that presented conquest as both necessary and benevolent. Drawing loosely on Darwin's theory of evolution, Social Darwinists argued that nations and races were locked in a struggle for survival in which the strong inevitably dominated the weak, making empire seem like a law of nature. Alongside this went the ideology of the 'civilizing mission' — the claim that Europeans had a duty to bring Christianity, education, and modern government to peoples deemed backward. These ideas served the practical interests of empire: they reassured voters at home, attracted missionaries and administrators to colonial service, and provided a moral cover for the seizure of land, labor, and resources.
—Historian's account of imperialist ideology in the period c. 1750–1900

q2.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Identify ONE claim Ferry makes about the rights of superior races.
parts.b: Describe ONE way in which Ferry connects colonial expansion to France's economic interests.
parts.c: Explain ONE reason why Ferry's arguments appealed to French republicans in the 1880s.

sample_answers.a: Ferry claims that superior races have not only a right but a duty to civilize inferior races, presenting colonial conquest as a moral obligation rather than mere aggression.
sample_answers.b: He argues that France's industrial economy needs colonial markets for its manufactured goods and sources of raw materials, and that without colonies France will decline into a minor power while rivals like Britain and Germany grow.
sample_answers.c: Republicans who opposed monarchy at home could support empire abroad because Ferry framed colonization as spreading republican civilization and universal values, allowing them to reconcile democratic ideals with imperial conquest.

q2.stimulus:
I repeat that the superior races have a right, because they have a duty. They have the duty to civilize the inferior races. ... In our time, I do not say that the great European powers are putting all their thought into it, but I observe that they are all turning toward colonial expansion. ... France must have a colonial policy: she has had one in all ages of her history. ... It is a question of markets. Our great industry, increasingly involved in foreign competition, must have outlets. If we do not do it, others will do it for us.
—Jules Ferry, speech to the French Chamber of Deputies, 1885

q3.directions: Use the image below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE feature of the advertisement that reflects imperialist attitudes toward colonized peoples.
parts.b: Explain ONE way in which the advertisement connects the sale of soap to the ideology of the 'civilizing mission.'
parts.c: Explain ONE reason why advertisements like this one were effective in building popular support for imperialism.

sample_answers.a: The ad shows a white child washing a Black child white (or the implication that soap — and by extension European civilization — can 'cleanse' non-Europeans), depicting colonized peoples as dirty or childlike and in need of European improvement.
sample_answers.b: By presenting soap as an instrument that literally whitens and civilizes, the ad turns a commercial product into a metaphor for empire: just as soap cleanses the body, European rule supposedly cleanses societies of backwardness.
sample_answers.c: Such ads reached millions of ordinary consumers in their homes, embedding imperialist assumptions into everyday life; people who might never read a political speech absorbed the message that empire was natural, benevolent, and tied to British commercial success.

q3.stimulus: The image is an 1899 British advertisement for Pears Soap, one of the most famous commercial images of the imperial era. The ad depicts a white child helping to wash a Black child, with the implication that the soap can wash away dark skin. Published at the height of the Scramble for Africa, the advertisement directly linked a household product to the ideology of the 'civilizing mission' — the claim that Europeans were uplifting colonized peoples.
